inlines.text: 摘要

blocks.text: 整个经济中的企业是如何采用 AI 的？它们遇到了哪些瓶颈和挑战？面对能力越来越强的模型，雇主该如何重新组织人的专业能力？为了更好地了解企业的实际体验，我们访谈了 Anthropic 的 58 家企业客户，共进行了 66 次访谈。我们发现：

inlines.text: 整个经济中的企业是如何采用 AI 的？它们遇到了哪些瓶颈和挑战？面对能力越来越强的模型，雇主该如何重新组织人的专业能力？为了更好地了解企业的实际体验，我们访谈了 Anthropic 的 58 家企业客户，共进行了 66 次访谈。我们发现：
AI 的价值来源。
企业正把 AI 部署到种类繁多、令人眼花缭乱的知识工作任务中。尤其是，它们越来越多地使用编程智能体，把软件能力带给非技术岗位。受访者表示，大多数 AI 应用是通过提升产出而非削减成本来创造价值的。他们认为这既因为 AI 加速了
现有
工作，也因为 AI 推动了新产品和新服务的改进。
对就业的影响。
在访谈中，我们几乎没有看到由 AI 自动化导致的国内裁员案例。尽管一些公司表示因为 AI 而增加了招聘，但多数公司表示因为 AI 而减少了招聘。许多公司还表示减少了对外包人员的聘用，尤其是海外外包人员。这些削减可能预示着国际商业服务行业即将出现就业冲击。
瓶颈。
企业报告了多种瓶颈，包括专家抵触 AI 部署，以及有些任务无法被 AI 加速。例如，随着编程速度加快，代码审查、销售和战略决策等其他任务越来越需要跟上节奏。
自上而下与自下而上两种路径的局限。
许多企业采用 AI 的方式是先确定一个可自动化的工作流程，再自上而下地推行解决方案。这种做法可能引发员工的不安全感、对职场监控的担忧，以及来自专家的抵触——而恰恰需要这些专家来搭建有效且持久的工作流程。另一些企业分发 AI 工具、等待自下而上的采用，确实看到了一些有价值的 AI 应用，但也面临采用不均衡、AI 只用于单一任务等瓶颈。
为 AI 重组组织。
受访者描述，价值最高的用法都涉及实质性的组织重组。一些企业拓宽员工的职责范围，让个人能够对完整的工作流程负责，并把员工调配到 AI 模型无法胜任的“瓶颈”任务上。一些企业还致力于赋能员工：搭建支持非开发者编程的基础设施，并在内部广泛开放业务数据。这些企业正在重组，以利用模型能力的持续提升，而不是固守一种假设 AI 工具将停留在当前水平的固定做法。

blocks.text: 大语言模型的应用正在经济各领域迅速铺开。人类组织围绕这些新奇协作者正在如何重塑自身？以我们采访过的一位中型律所员工为例。多年来，这家律所的收发室一直遵循同一套流程：扫描仪把收到的信件转成 PDF 发到一个收件箱；邮件文员逐个打开 PDF，快速浏览，点击“另存为”，重命名，再放进律所的文件系统。每封信要花五分钟。有一天，一位资深开发者来到收发室，观察信件处理过程。一个月后，他做出了一套 AI 系统，最终简化为两次 API 调用：先根据文档首页为其命名，再在律所文档系统中为它分配位置。收发室的文员们“都惊呆了”。

blocks.text: 我们采访的另一家律所里，有位员工希望 AI 能为律所打造“第二大脑”。（“对于更高层次的工作，它只是打开了各种可能性。”）但这家律所很难让所有人都高效地用上 AI。发给潜在被告的索赔函里塞满了过多的破折号，还时不时出错。开发应用的律师总是“撞上幻觉出来的、根本不存在的菜单或按钮”。其他人则担心保密和数据安全，或者干脆“没时间登上这趟 AI 列车”。少数重度用户用 AI 生成的文章把律所淹没了，“随手就给 IT 团队发去 Claude 提示词生成的七页指令”。

blocks.text: 我们采访的第三家律所很早就采用了 AI，使用率很高。该所早期项目之一是一套 AI 计时系统，帮律师省去了记录计费工时的麻烦。IT 员工看到自己的一部分工作被自动化了，但随后转而专注于搭建安全的基础设施来托管应用、管理上下文，为律所其他部门服务。随着 AI 工具普及，律所意识到，某些法律文书初稿已经不再需要由初级律师来写。可如果不写初稿，“初级律师怎么判断这份稿子是好是坏？”于是律所推出了一套新流程：年轻律师“必须真正拿着这份[AI 写的]初稿，和资深律师一起处理”，两人结对，共同批注、修改这份初稿。

blocks.text: 这三家律所在同一行业应用了同样的技术，方式却各不相同。第一家自动化了一套工作流程，提升了效率，却让收发室文员面临失业风险。第二家因为采用和有效落地的瓶颈，既没有造成岗位消失，也削弱了本可让律所受益的生产力提升。第三家则重组了工作，没有裁掉任何岗位，因为要有效使用这项技术，就必须把员工重新部署到新任务上。律所重新设计了角色，让人的专业能力得以保留，成为能力日益强大的 AI 模型的补充。

blocks.text: 本文基于在美国 58 家公司开展的 66 场面对面访谈，探讨 AI 驱动的价值与工作重组之间的联系。这些公司都正处于采用 AI 的过程中。我们访谈了高管、管理者和一线员工，既有 AI 原生初创公司，也有百年老店；既有制造商，也有科技公司。我们与结构工程师、牙医、会计师交流，也走访了对冲基金、律师事务所和私募股权公司的员工，还有一位物业经理、一家卡车运输公司和一家出版商。他们都是 Anthropic 的客户，但许多人同时也在使用其他 AI 工具。之所以选择他们参与本研究，是因为他们在行业、规模和 AI 使用程度上分布广泛，不过他们并非随机样本，也不具备系统代表性。

blocks.text: 最有价值的应用之所以带来显著的组织变革，原因有几点。有些情况下，AI 应用要取得成功就必须进行结构性调整，比如必须澄清某项政策，AI 智能体才能在评估工作流中严格执行它。另一些情况下，初步成功激发了进一步推进更大规模组织变革、以更充分利用 AI 的热情。还有一些情况下，使用 AI 的成功倒逼了下游环节的改变。一家商业地产公司发现，员工开始自行向客户发送文件。但这意味着他们违反了公司规定——对外材料须经由市场部门发出。正如一位 IT 总监所解释的：“这挺好，嘿，我们又多了一个客户。但这也不好，因为我们的标准操作流程开始瓦解了。”这些故事与学术研究相呼应：要从变革性技术中获取价值，组织变革必不可少。

inlines.text: 拓宽岗位职责

blocks.text: 企业拓宽员工职责后，个人要对整个工作流程负责，而不是只负责某一狭窄的专业领域。例如，工程师可能开始跨产品、设计甚至客户互动开展工作。一家医疗健康初创公司要求所有工程师——不只是业务人员——定期与使用其产品的医疗专业人士交流。让一名员工或一个小团队负责整个产品或客户关系，可以减少组织摩擦和潜在的否决，否则这些因素会阻碍 AI 加速落地。正如一位工程负责人所说：“两个人加上 Claude，效果惊人……只要两个人达成一致，直接发布就行。”

blocks.text: 随着生产速度加快——不仅是代码生产，还包括法律研究、数据分析、财务建模等知识工作的其他方面——在整个组织内就“要做什么”达成一致可能变得缓慢且成本高昂。但单个个人或小团队对整个工作流程的控制越强，这些协调成本就越不明显。一位高管谈到重新设计线索获取、客户主管和客户成功等岗位，将它们合并为一个负责整个客户生命周期的角色。AI 工具让跟进交易流程中每一步的细节变得更容易，也让把任务交给同事所导致的“上下文丢失”代价更高。一位初创公司创始人表示，公司只聘用个人贡献者，并让每个人负责产品和业务中一个独立的部分。在另一家公司，一位经理解释说：“我们实际上把设计师、产品经理、工程师、QA 甚至基础设施合并成一个角色。”另一位工程负责人则致力于“让工程师与客户有更多全身心的接触”。图 5 展示了岗位从特定职能向整个工作流程拓宽的例子。

blocks.text: 面对 AI 带来的加速，一些公司的应对方式是把员工调配到仍是瓶颈的任务上。如果员工能去攻克瓶颈，就能更好地补足 AI 模型的能力。还记得那位软件工程师 Ellen 吗？她起初担心自己会被编程智能体取代。她最终接受了“整个工作已经从写代码变成了做决策”。在一家咨询公司，咨询顾问帮助把相互冲突的最佳实践和标准文档的核对流程自动化了。随后，这些顾问转向了更多“人与人之间的咨询工作，而不是翻查文档”。同样，一位工程总监建议团队多花时间“和你的 PM（产品经理）沟通，帮 PM 针对用户旅程提出相关问题”。一位运营负责人说，自动化让他们“有更多时间做流程变革和争取支持。说实话，那才是最大的硬仗——流程变革”。在这些案例中，工作都转向了限制模型生产力的人际沟通和战略性任务。

blocks.text: 或许最重要的共享基础设施是公司数据，它为日益自主的智能体和跨职能员工提供上下文。有了AI，高管可以在“需要的那一刻”查询业务数据，而不必等待数据分析师的定期报告。一家卡车运输公司搭建了一个智能体可访问的“数据仓库”，公司各地的管理者开始基于这些数据自行做分析：“他们完全迷上了它，”该公司的一位人士说。不再由商业智能或数据科学团队来中转每一次分析请求——“那本来会排进队列，有时要等上一两年”——大量知识工作者开始自己运行SQL查询。在另一家公司，一个销售团队一头扎进数据分析，把销售和财务数据关联起来：“谁都能做。所以现在大家都在做。”一位员工说，如果没有AI，“他们可能永远都看不到[这些数据]，或者永远不会尝试用这些数据做任何事。”而一家在线交易平台的可信与安全团队则用他们新的数据分析工具来识别欺诈模式。正如一位团队成员所解释的：“我们[现在]可以解析我们所有的日志了。”这些例子都取决于公司首先把数据汇入并整合起来，让AI拥有所需的上下文。这与先前关于企业应用的研究一致：该研究发现，越复杂的任务往往越需要用户提供更多上下文（以输入token衡量）。

blocks.text: 结论

inlines.text: 结论

blocks.text: 我们访谈的数十人都表示，AI 已经在他们公司大量自动化了一系列工作，尤其是在软件工程、客户服务和后台岗位上。但我们也听到了各种瓶颈，它们使某些任务上的效率提升无法转化为企业的整体收益。正如一位高管所说：“你离钱越近，模型就越难在那项工作上表现出色。”如果原型制作很快但部署很慢，或者生产很快但营销很慢，那么 AI 工具带来的实际效果就远不及模型评测和能力所显示的水平。

blocks.text: 与 AI 协同工作的人面临更深层的问题。在自上而下的部署中，自动化和监控有可能损害员工利益。在自下而上的部署中，组织内部推进速度不一致，会导致员工之间或团队之间的绩效不平等。

inlines.text: How are businesses across the economy adopting AI? What bottlenecks and challenges have they faced? How can employers reorganize human expertise around increasingly capable models? To understand businesses’ experiences better, we conducted 66 interviews with 58 of Anthropic’s enterprise customers. We found:
Sources of AI value.

Companies are deploying AI across a dizzying range of knowledge work tasks. In particular, they are increasingly using coding agents to bring software capabilities to nontechnical roles. Interviewees report that most uses of AI add value by increasing their output, rather than by cutting costs. They attribute this both to AI accelerating
existing
work and to its role in introducing novel product and service improvements.
Impact on employment.

Across our interviews, we saw very few examples of domestic layoffs that were driven by AI automation. Although some companies reported hiring more due to AI, most companies reported hiring less due to AI. Many also reported reducing their use of contractors, particularly offshore ones. These reported cuts could be an early warning of job disruption in the international business services industry.
Bottlenecks.

Companies reported a range of bottlenecks, including experts resisting AI deployment and tasks that are not accelerated by AI. As coding speeds up, for example, other tasks—like code review, sales, and strategic decision-making—increasingly need to keep pace.
Limits to top-down and bottom-up approaches.

Many companies approach AI by identifying a workflow to automate and rolling out a top-down solution. This approach can lead to job insecurity, fears of workplace surveillance, and resistance from the experts needed to set up an effective and durable workflow. Companies that distribute AI tools and wait for bottom-up adoption see some valuable AI use but face bottlenecks from unequal adoption and single-task AI implementations.
Reorganizing for AI.

Interviewees described the highest-value uses as involving meaningful reorganization. Some companies are broadening their employees’ roles to ensure individuals can take ownership over whole workflows, and are redeploying employees to the “bottleneck” tasks that AI models cannot do. Some also seek to empower employees by building out infrastructure to support nondeveloper coding and by providing broad-based internal access to business data. These companies are reorganizing to take advantage of ongoing model capability improvements rather than settling on a fixed approach that assumes AI tools will remain as powerful as they are today.

blocks.text: The use of LLMs has exploded across the economy. How are human organizations reshaping around these strange new collaborators? Consider an employee at a midsize law firm that we spoke to. For years, the firm’s mailroom had followed the same protocol: a scanner sent PDFs of incoming correspondence to an inbox; a mail clerk opened each PDF, skimmed it, clicked “Save As,” renamed it, and placed it in the firm’s file system. The process took five minutes per letter. One day, a senior developer visited the mailroom to watch the mail being processed. In a month, he built an AI system that eventually became two API calls, which name the document based on its first page and then assign it a place in the firm’s document system. The mail clerks “were blown away.”

blocks.text: In this article, we explore the connections between AI-driven value and work reorganization through 66 face-to-face interviews conducted across 58 companies in the US, all of which are in the midst of adopting AI. We interviewed executives, managers, and individual contributors. We talked to employees at AI-native startups and 100-year-old businesses. We interviewed people at manufacturers and tech companies. We spoke with structural engineers, dentists, and accountants; employees at hedge funds, law firms, and private equity firms; a property manager, a trucking company, and a publisher. They’re all Anthropic customers, but many also use other AI tools. They were selected for this study because of their range across industry, size, and AI usage, though they are not a random or systematically representative sample.

blocks.text: There are several reasons why the most valuable applications led to significant organizational change. In some cases, the AI applications required a structural change in order to be successful, such as when a policy had to be clarified so that AI agents could rigorously apply it in an assessment workflow. In other cases, initial success spurred excitement about making larger organizational changes to further harness AI. In others, the success of using AI forced downstream changes. One commercial real estate company saw its staff start sending out client-facing documents themselves. But this meant they had violated company rules that asked employees to route external materials through the marketing department. As an IT director explained, “That’s good because, hey, we got another client. That’s bad because our standard operating procedures are starting to fall apart.” These stories echo academic research that shows that organizational change is necessary to derive value from transformative technologies.

blocks.text: Mark’s fears were understandable—and far from unique. This past year, AI has loomed especially large in performance assessments across industries. Some of the most sobering moments in our interviews were when managers described making difficult decisions to terminate employees who wouldn’t adopt AI. (By contrast, 10 companies reported hiring more due to AI, primarily into AI implementation roles and to bolster IT support, and others had grown rapidly for a variety of business reasons.) But layoffs weren’t the only adverse employment effect. People at two-thirds of the companies we spoke to reported reduced hiring due to AI: as one person put it, “We may not be firing, but we’re not hiring.” A third of these hiring declines were due to companies actively shrinking functions through attrition without backfilling the roles. blocks.text: Top-down deployments like these shift power from employees to executives and owners. But they can also be brittle, because they can quickly become out of date or obsolete. For example, the dozens of performance dimensions that customer service representatives were rated on are scored by a two-year-old model and are not taken seriously by managers. inlines.text: Broadening roles

blocks.text: When firms broaden employees’ roles, individuals become responsible for an entire workflow rather than one narrow type of expertise. Engineers, for example, might start working across product, design, and even customer engagement. One healthcare startup asked all of its engineers—not just its business people—to speak regularly to medical professionals who used their product. Having a single employee or small team own an entire product or customer relationship limits the organizational friction and potential vetoes that can otherwise block AI acceleration. As one engineering leader put it, “Two people plus Claude is the most amazing thing… if two people agree on something, just ship it.”

blocks.text: Another benefit of role broadening is that even as some parts of a job are automated, experts have less reason to fear job loss. At current model capabilities, agentic workflows still typically need active expert engagement and input to develop. They also require ongoing maintenance as models improve and workflows change. For example, one engineer automated a system to respond to production-alert tickets, which had previously been a substantial part of his job. For two months after deploying the system, the engineer read transcripts of every conversation with the AI agent and tweaked the prompts, repaired broken integrations, supplied missing vendor documentation, and approved agents’ authorization requests. Six months in, with the system working well, he still sampled transcripts every two weeks to update and maintain the system. He also kept building on it. The alert agent became a company-wide Slack agent (“the company basically runs on it now”), and then an agent that keeps skills and context up to date on everyone’s laptop.

blocks.text: Redeploying employees toward bottleneck tasks

inlines.text: Redeploying employees toward bottleneck tasks

blocks.text: Some companies respond to AI-enabled acceleration by shifting employees toward the tasks that are still bottlenecks. If employees can chase down bottlenecks, they can better complement the capabilities of AI models. Recall Ellen, the software engineer who was initially afraid she would lose her job to coding agents. She eventually accepted that “the entire job has switched right from writing code to making decisions.” At a consulting company, consultants helped automate the process of reconciling best practices and standards documents that conflicted with one another. The consultants then shifted to more “person-to-person consulting work instead of sifting through documents.” Likewise, an engineering director suggested that their team spend more time “talking to your PM [product manager] and helping your PM raise relevant questions against the user journey.” An operations leader said automation gave them “more time for the process change and the buy-in. Honestly, that is the biggest battle—that process change.” In these cases, the work shifted toward the interpersonal and strategic tasks that limit models’ productivity.

blocks.text: As another example, project managers at a construction company contributed to an agentic workflow for checking in across construction sites. Previously, project managers would call crew members at different sites every morning, put notes together, and write up a daily report for customers. As the CTO put it, “Claude is a terrible product manager... So it’s a lot of taste deciding what features are important.”

As software development becomes the purview of a whole gamut of nontechnical functions, engineers broaden their scope across design, product management, and even core business functions. Production planners, accustomed to poring over spreadsheets, become data labelers, providing qualitative context for AI agents to better understand the numbers: “You should be a journalist… you should not think about competing with AI.”

blocks.text: Building common infrastructure

inlines.text: Building common infrastructure

blocks.text: Several companies have set up common infrastructure that allows nontechnical people to build apps that do not expose security vulnerabilities or require substantial maintenance by engineers. “Every single employee now is a developer… creating additional attack surface every day,” a data security executive told us. The head of engineering at a real estate company said they “went from having a team of five developers to a team of [dozens of] developers that all want to release software.”

blocks.text: Perhaps the most important shared infrastructure is company data, which provides context both for increasingly autonomous agents and for employees across functions. With AI, an executive can query business data “at the moment of need” rather than waiting for a regular report from data analysts. A trucking company built an agent-accessible “data warehouse,” and managers across the company began creating their own analyses based on that data: “they’re absolutely addicted to it,” a person at the company said. Instead of a business intelligence or data science team mediating every request for analysis—“it would have ended up on the queue, sometimes a year or two”—a broad range of knowledge workers started running SQL queries themselves. At another company, a sales team leapt into data analysis, linking sales and finance data: “Anybody can do it. And so now everybody does it.” Without AI, one employee said, “they probably would have never seen [the data], or they would have never tried to do anything with it.” And the trust and safety team at an online marketplace used their new data analytics tools to identify fraud patterns. As one team member explained, “we can [now] go parse through all of our logs.” These examples all depended on companies first pulling in and consolidating their data so that AI had the context it needed. This is consistent with prior research on enterprise use, which found that more complex tasks tend to require more context from users (measured in input tokens).

blocks.text: Conclusion

inlines.text: Conclusion

blocks.text: The dozens of people we interviewed told us that AI has substantially automated a range of work at their companies, particularly in software engineering, customer service, and back-office roles. But we also heard about a variety of bottlenecks that prevented productivity gains on particular tasks from translating into overall benefits for businesses. As one executive put it, “The closer you are to the money, the harder it is for models to excel in that job.” If prototyping is fast but deployment is not, or production is fast but marketing is slow, then AI tools deliver far less than model evaluations and capabilities would imply.

blocks.text: Companies that reorganized around AI addressed the challenges associated with both top-down and bottom-up approaches. Interpersonal and strategic tasks are currently the central bottlenecks where humans are needed, but the details of these roles will continue to change as models improve. blocks.text: How can employers deliver on this potential? Our interviews suggest that some companies are already sharing the gains of AI deployments with their employees, using productivity gains to improve job quality and lighten tedious work. Sharing the gains in this way may also motivate employees to contribute their expertise to redesigning workflows for AI tools. Companies that commit to internal worker reallocation must plan ahead for where those workers could go. And they can give employees, including nontechnical ones, broad access to the data and infrastructure they need to make the most of new AI tools. Finally, model developers like Anthropic must support these practices by offering training and help to business customers. We hope the findings in this report will inform those efforts.
